We derive bounds relating the measure to weighted pairwise distributional distances and population diversity across ranks, and examine the contributions of the minimum and maximum, obtaining a simple expression for two populations. Monte Carlo simulations with four populations assess its finite-sample behavior and asymptotic convergence. The empirical application reveals a shift in heterogeneity toward higher ranks in the germ-free group.

title: Bayesian Time-Varying Spectral Estimation for LISA with P-Splines
abstract: We model the evolutionary spectrum of a slowly time-varying process by a linear combination of products of time- and frequency-dependent B-splines, placing a Gaussian tensor-product penalty prior on the coefficients. The posterior distribution is obtained by updating the prior using a Whittle-type likelihood approximation of the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer time-frequency coefficients. Separate regularisation in time and frequency allows non-stationary spectral structure to be inferred. An adaptive coarse-grained likelihood reduces the computational cost while preserving fine resolution around sharp spectral features. We first validate the method using repeated simulations of a locally stationary process with known spectrum, showing lower reconstruction errors and narrower posterior intervals as the sample size increases. We then apply it to a year-long simulated LISA data set with stationary instrumental single link spectra, an evolving time-delay interferometry (TDI) response, and a modulated Galactic foreground. We compare a flexible total power spectral density (PSD) model with models incorporating progressively stronger physical information and examine both continuous and gapped observations. Allowing time variation substantially improves reconstruction relative to a stationary model, while incorporating physical information about the TDI response further improves recovery, particularly near its moving spectral features. The results illustrate the trade-off between spectral flexibility, physical assumptions, and posterior uncertainty in non-stationary LISA noise estimation.

title: Spreads Don't Price a Rival Market Maker's Information
abstract: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads? Adverse-selection reasoning suggests that they should, because the better-informed maker avoids toxic order flow and leaves more of it to the others, and the closest model of competition with an informed dealer predicts more conservative quotes by the uninformed dealers. We study this question in a stochastic quoting game in which one maker receives a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state that drives order flow. Strategies are learned with independent reinforcement learning, which we benchmark against an exact dynamic-programming solution of the single-agent case. In none of the configurations we examine does the average spread of the uninformed makers increase with the rival's precision. Where competition for order flow is weak, the slope of their spread in precision is statistically equivalent to zero within half an action tick; where competition is strong, their spread tightens. The informed maker's own spread tightens markedly in every configuration and serves as a positive control. These results hold with two, three and four makers, across an eightfold variation in the depth of the background liquidity, with a background quote that reprices after toxic fills, and under price-time priority. Our measurements point to a competitive trade-off. In the model the total toxicity of the flow does not depend on any maker's information. A better-informed maker avoids more of it, and where this leaves more toxic flow to its competitors, it also quotes more tightly, so that a wider quote would cost them more order flow than it would save in adverse selection. The uninformed makers adjust the skew of their quotes and their inventory instead, and the rival's information changes the distribution of profits across makers while quoted spreads remain nearly unchanged.

title: Unit-Level Conformal Inference for Panel Counterfactuals
abstract: We develop conformal inference for panel counterfactual estimators using the exchangeability of prediction errors across units rather than over time. Existing conformal methods for panels with few treated units rely on temporal properties of treated-unit residuals, which are vulnerable to strong temporal heterogeneity such as nonstationarity. We instead hold out each control unit, hide its relevant outcomes, and predict them using the same rule applied to the treated unit. Target-date estimators, including difference-in-differences and synthetic control, use controls' pre-treatment and target-date outcomes to construct the counterfactual, allowing both full conformal confidence sets and Jackknife+ intervals. Full-path estimators, including factor-model imputation and matrix completion, also use controls' outcomes at other post-treatment dates; for these, we use the Jackknife+. Both procedures yield finite-sample, period-wise confidence sets under this across-unit exchangeability, without requiring stationarity or random assignment. We characterize when the coverage holds and show why a common prediction rule alone does not ensure it. For multiple treated units, a block Jackknife+ covers their average effect, while a relabeling test is exact for sharp nulls over all treated cells. We show that the synthetic control placebo test is a full conformal test of no effect that extends to full-path estimators. We also relate our procedures to a parametric bootstrap and classify common estimators by the inference they allow. We illustrate our procedures in three empirical applications.

title: Learning the Average Dose-Response Function with a Right-Censored Treatment
abstract: This paper considers estimation and inference for the average dose-response function under right-censored treatment duration and missing outcomes for censored units. Using the duration lower bounds provided by censored records, we construct a novel multiply robust estimator through augmented local estimating equations. Under suitable regularity conditions, the estimator remains consistent when any two of the outcome regression, treatment density, and censoring survival function are consistently estimated. We establish its convergence rate and asymptotic distribution within a cross-fitting framework under appropriate conditions on nuisance estimation. To address local smoothing bias that can distort confidence interval coverage, we further develop a debiased estimator that supports asymptotically valid pointwise inference without undersmoothing. Under additional uniform conditions, we construct simultaneous confidence bands using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Simulation studies evaluate estimation accuracy, the validity of pointwise and uniform inference, and robustness to nuisance model misspecification. A semi-synthetic study calibrated to NHANES illustrates the proposed methods in a setting with a known dose-response function.

title: Bayesian Inference for Multivariate Stable Distributions via LePage Representation with von Mises -- Fisher Spectral Measure
abstract: We develop Bayesian inference for multivariate $\alpha$-stable distributions with von Mises--Fisher spectral measure, motivated by the hitting distribution of Brownian motion on the unit sphere. Inference proceeds via a LePage-type series representation with latent radial, spectral, and Poisson components; truncation bias is absorbed through a Gaussian error term, yielding a likelihood that is smooth in $\alpha\in(0,2)$ with no special treatment at the Cauchy boundary $\alpha=1$. The stability index $\alpha$, spectral concentration $\kappa$, mean direction $\eta$, and spectral mass $\Gamma_\infty$ are estimated jointly by Markov chain Monte Carlo. At the Gaussian boundary $\alpha\to 2$, the limiting covariance matrix equals twice the second moment matrix of the spectral measure, with explicit parametric form determined by $\eta$ and $\kappa$; in particular, the anisotropy of the limiting Gaussian distribution is controlled solely by the spectral concentration $\kappa$. Simulation across $\alpha\in[0.25, 1.99]$ confirms reliable recovery of all parameters.

title: Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations
abstract: This paper develops computational algorithms for testing discrete-choice random utility models (RUM). The set of RUM-consistent choice probabilities forms a polytope, and existing computational methods rely on its vertex representation. We exploit alternative half-space (Block--Marschak inequalities) and network-flow representations to develop two methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers and a flow-based column-generation algorithm. Compared with current vertex-based methods, our algorithms are better suited to GPU implementation. We establish convergence guarantees and provide optimality certificates for all three algorithms. The resulting algorithms achieve $100$--$600\times$ speedups over existing methods. The solver based on our methods is publicly available on Github at \href{https://github.com/mingxiz/d-rum-testing-gpu}{\texttt{d-rum-testing-gpu}}.

title: Estimation of Heterogeneous and Functional Cox Model
abstract: Cox or proportional hazards model is the most commonly used regression model for failure time data and has been extended in various ways. In this paper, we consider inference for a heterogeneous and functional Cox model with the focus on estimation of the latent heterogeneous or subgroup structure based on interval-censored failure time data. For the problem, we propose a novel sieve maximum likelihood estimation procedure with the uses of B-splines and Bernstein polynomials. For the implementation of the proposed method, an EM algorithm is developed and the number of subgroups can be determined in a data-driven manner. Also the resulting estimators are shown to be consistent and asymptotically normal, and an extensive simulation study shows that the proposed method works well in practice. Finally, we apply it to an Alzheimer's Disease study that motivated this investigation and provide some new insights about the roles of imaging and clinical factors in the progression of Alzheimer's disease.

title: Estimating Hessian Log-Determinants without Forming the Hessian Matrix
authors: Geng Zhang and James C. Spall
abstract: The log-determinant of a positive-definite Hessian matrix is used in uncertainty assessment, Bayesian model comparison, and experimental design. Computing this quantity can be difficult when function values are available but derivatives are not. We combine simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation with stochastic Lanczos quadrature (SPSA-SLQ) to estimate the log-determinant without forming the Hessian. Possibly noisy function values suffice for fixed-data and expected Hessians, including Fisher information matrices. We derive a local bound on log-determinant error due to Hessian-vector product approximation, quadrature, and averaging random probes. Three numerical studies examine accuracy and computational cost. In a 3002-parameter example, SPSA-SLQ gives a relative root-mean-square error below 1% and uses 65% less peak GPU memory than a basic full-matrix estimator. A sensor-placement study also compares improved full-matrix methods and evaluates layout selection.

title: GENMETA-Lite: A Fast and Flexible Approach to Federated Learning with Disparate Covariate Information Across Studies
abstract: Meta-analysis is foundational to federated learning, where one learns parameters by combining information across studies without sharing individual-level data. Handling missing and disparate covariates across studies is a major issue due to potential introduction of bias and decreased efficiency. We previously proposed a generalized meta-analysis estimator (GENMETA) to build a unified regression model using information on parameter estimates from sub-models and a reference population to estimate the joint covariate distribution. Building on that work, we present a linear estimator (GENMETA-Lite) as a practical, non-iterative method for multivariate meta-analysis, extended to handle heterogeneity in covariate distributions across studies, coarsened covariates, and model selection. Simulations demonstrate that our estimator has robust performance compared to estimates from na\"ive inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis or multiple imputation with individual-level data (approximately 4 to 100-fold reduction in mean squared error), even when underlying assumptions of linearity and homogeneous distributions are violated. We apply the method to fit a breast cancer risk prediction model with data from five studies (N = 313,851). Our study shows GENMETA-Lite is a robust federated learning approach for building regression models by combining information across disparate studies. An R package implementing these methods is made publicly available.

title: A Bias-Variance Framework for Estimating Stochastic Speed-Density Relationship Considering Constrained Sample Size
abstract: Accurate calibration of traffic speed-density fundamental diagram models is essential for freeway traffic flow analysis, yet existing approaches estimate parameters from fixed datasets without examining how estimates evolve as data availability increases. This study develops a comprehensive Bayesian stochastic calibration framework integrating sequential Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation via a Metropolis-Hastings within Gibbs sampling scheme with a novel Bias-Variance Cone analysis for asymptotic parameter identification. The framework is applied to 17 macroscopic speed-density models using one full year of 5-minute PeMS loop detector data from three California freeway stations. Sequential MCMC progressively increases the number of randomly sampled days from 1 to 365, enabling systematic evaluation of parameter stability and convergence as a function of data availability. Among the 17 models, nine achieved stable posterior convergence with physically interpretable estimates, while four exhibited catastrophic structural failures due to logarithmic singularities, unit incompatibilities, and initialization sensitivity. The Bias-Variance Cone framework, representing the first application of asymptotic bias-variance decomposition to fundamental diagram calibration, establishes that free-flow speed parameters are reliably identified within approximately 30 days, whereas density and shape parameters require 100 to 182 days, providing the first quantitative minimum data requirements in the literature. Collectively, the findings provide an empirical identifiability ranking of 17 fundamental diagram models, a validated minimum data sufficiency framework, and a replicable, automated platform for large-scale stochastic fundamental diagram calibration.

title: Corporate Stances on Societal Issues in the US
abstract: When do firms take public positions on divisive societal issues and why? We assemble a comprehensive dataset on corporate stance-taking in the United States, using large language models to read 52,000 news articles and press releases about 836 companies that belonged to the S&P 500 at any point between 2008 and 2025. We identify 9,917 stances on nine partisan issues such as climate change, abortion, and racial discrimination. We show that stance-taking increased fourfold after 2008 and peaked in 2021. It is overwhelmingly liberal and concentrated among the largest firms. A quarter of stances give no explicit business justification. Stance-taking is only weakly related to lobbying and campaign contributions and, unlike them, does not follow the electoral cycle. Instead, firms tend to speak when media coverage and public interest in an issue peak. Together, these findings suggest that stance-taking can be understood as a contribution to broad policy debates rather than a strategy to shape policies that affect firms' core business. Finally, we investigate whose views corporate stances represent. Consumer-facing firms take more stances, and firms whose consumers lean Democratic take more liberal stances on issues other than climate. Companies with larger shares of Democratic employees, executives, and board members also take more liberal stances. Exploiting within-firm variation, we find that having more Democrats among a company's leadership increases liberal stance-taking, while having more women increases stance-taking on gender-related issues and abortion.

title: Log-optimal two-sample testing by betting
abstract: For each standard Borel observation space, we construct a single anytime-valid two-sample procedure that is asymptotically log-optimal for every pair of unknown probability laws and every limiting ratio of diverging sample sizes, including zero and infinity. For independent balanced pairs, the optimal log-wealth rate is $2\JS(P,Q)$, where $\JS$ is the Jensen--Shannon divergence. Unequal sizes yield weighted Jensen--Shannon information and the one-sample limit $\log W(n_1,n_2)/n_2\to\KL(Q\|P)$ when $n_1/n_2\to\infty$. Refining finite partitions and logarithmic-loss learning with measurable characteristic kernels provide universal constructions. Our main contribution is the generality of our construction, and its connections to classical batch efficiency notions. Practical implementations allow continuous classifier fine-tuning, as demonstrated on finite alphabets, Gaussian data, and handwritten digits.

title: Aggregating Rankings of Coalitions to Rank Individuals
abstract: We develop an ordinal framework for aggregating a profile of rankings of coalitional performances to determine the ranking of individuals. From university ratings to the assessment of team-sports players, we often evaluate individuals based on their coalitional performances. Although such evaluation has been addressed by cooperative game theory, it is only recently that its ordinal counterpart, social ranking theory (Moretti, 2015), has emerged. As most of the literature considers a single coalitional ranking (which corresponds to a real-valued characteristic function), we extend the model to allow a profile of coalitional rankings (which corresponds to a multidimensional characteristic function). We tackle the aggregation problem by introducing three families of inter-profile axioms, each representing how the rankings should interact or contribute to the output. After revealing fundamental impossibilities concerning the reconciliation of different families, we characterize a new solution, Pareto-extension Lex-cel (PEL), via some weaker versions of the inter-profile axioms. PEL extends Lex-cel, which is a central solution in social ranking theory, by analogy with Sen's Pareto extension rule. Our results develop the connection between classical Arrovian aggregation, cooperative game theory, and social ranking theory.

title: Rank Functions of Flag Matroids with Applications to Order-Neutral Submodular Valuations
abstract: We provide a rank function axiomatization for flag matroids and show that it is cryptomorphic to the definition of flag matroids as a sequence of matroid quotients. Afterwards, we present some applications of flag matroid rank functions by providing solutions to selected problems. In particular, we discuss connections between flag matroids and submodular valuations in computational economics by showing that rank functions of flag matroids of length $k$ are precisely the same as $\{0, 1, \dots, k\}$-order-neutral submodular valuations. We then prove that $v:2^E\to \mathbb{R}$ is an order-neutral submodular valuation if and only if $v$ can be written as $v(X) = b|X| + \sum_{i=1}^l c_ir_{N_i}(X), \quad b \in \mathbb{R}, c_i > 0$, where $N_{i+1}$ is a quotient of $N_i$. Doing so allows us to prove that every order-neutral submodular valuation is a gross-substitute valuation and that not every order-neutral submodular valuation is a Rado valuation. Furthermore, we prove that if $|E|\geq 3$, then a set $A$ is a Sidon set if and only if all $A$-submodular valuations are order-neutral, if and only if all $A$-submodular valuations are gross-substitute valuations.

title: A Distributionally Robust Framework for Safe and Generalizable Utilization of Surrogate Markers
abstract: Surrogate endpoints can accelerate treatment evaluation, but their validity is challenging to establish because the joint distribution of counterfactual outcome surrogate pairs is not identifiable. We propose a distributionally robust framework for safe and generalizable surrogate evaluation that explicitly accounts for this uncertainty. By treating cross arm dependence as partially identified, we formulate a maximin optimization problem that learns an optimal surrogate transformation by maximizing the worst case explained variance of individual treatment effects over admissible counterfactual dependence structures. The resulting robust surrogacy measure provides a conservative lower bound on explained treatment effect variation. Moreover, our maximin construction guarantees nonnegative alignment between the treatment effects on the transformed surrogate and the primary outcome over the admissible counterfactual couplings. To generalize surrogacy evaluation across populations under covariate shift, we integrate transfer learning with debiased machine learning to estimate the required target population moments using source trial data and target baseline covariates. The computational tractability and asymptotic properties of our method are established. Simulations demonstrate good finite sample performance and show that the proposed method guards against counterfactual misalignment by shrinking the learned transformation toward zero, revealing a robustness prediction tradeoff. We illustrate the framework by evaluating 18 month glomerular filtration rate change as a surrogate for two year change using multiple randomized clinical trial data sets.

title: Community Odour Reports as a Forecastable Sensor of Fugitive Emissions
abstract: Ambient air quality monitors (AAQMs) measure exposure to emissions from waste facilities at few points; for most residents the only record is their own odour reports, used by regulators as evidence of impact but not typically as measurements of exposure. Calibrated public reports are accepted measurements in seismology, but whether community odour reports can serve as a sensor of exposure, and be forecast, is untested against independent monitors. Here we show they can, at a UK landfill, with SENTINEL, which combines the public weather forecast, run through a dispersion model, with the reports already received and no instrument at the site. Judged against the independent monitors, monthly report frequency was correlated with hydrogen sulphide (r = 0.92) and daily reports remained associated with it beyond weather; they fell fourteenfold after a change at the source while modelled transport did not; and, with no gas data as input, gave exposure in both monitored postcodes within a factor of three of that measured. SENTINEL forecast daily report counts with skill 0.64 one day and 0.50 four days ahead, exceeding damped persistence four days ahead; the one-day gain over persistence was unresolved. Community odour reports can act as a relative sensor complementing sparse monitoring; a monitor is needed for absolute scale.

title: From Viral Exposure to Engagement: A Causal Mediation Framework for Digital Platforms
abstract: At Roblox, viral hits can change how exposed players engage with the viral game and with the rest of the platform. We develop a causal mediation framework to decompose the effect of viral-game playtime on subsequent player engagement into a direct effect and indirect effects through measured player interaction and discovery behaviors. The framework uses a causal DAG to state the assumed causal structure and a time-ordered design that measures covariates, exposure, mediators, and outcomes in non-overlapping time windows. Under stated identification assumptions and a model linear in the exposure and each mediator at fixed covariates, we estimate every path as a function of player covariates with cross-fitted R-learners, which use only prediction models and therefore scale to platform-size data. Averaging the fitted surfaces inherits their regularization bias, so we add a per-player bias correction before averaging (Chernozhukov et al., 2018). In simulation, the correction restored nominal coverage of 90% to 95%, against at most 39% for intervals built by averaging the surfaces. Counterintuitively, interval coverage worsened with more data on a difficult mediator-outcome path, bias shrank more slowly than the standard error, reducing corrected coverage from 93.6% to 57.3% as n increased from 2k to 200k. We applied the same design to two de-identified viral games with different lifecycle histories, comparing effects across outcome scopes, player subgroups, and a placebo window without a viral event. The results indicate that subsequent engagement is not explained by viral exposure alone, player interaction behaviors mediate 46% engagement within the viral game, whereas new game discovery mediates 52% engagement in other games. Finally, we compare the estimator with its alternatives and generalize the study design into a reusable framework for similar mediation studies across product domains.

title: Modeling Risks with Masked Causes and Variable Exposure
abstract: Cohort studies and surveys often record how much time each subject spent under each of two or several treatment conditions and whether an event occurred, but not the condition under which it occurred. We develop two models for such data, for binary and count outcomes. Both start with events under each treatment condition as independent Poisson counts, and estimate rate ratios between treatment and control conditions. In the binary model, only an indicator of any event is observed, and the event probability under each condition follows a complementary log-log model with a log-exposure offset; development is done for general link functions, including log and logit. The interpretation of the treatment effect changes accordingly. In the count model, the number of events combined over all treatment conditions is observed; overdispersion is handled by Pearson scaling. Parameters are estimated either by the expectation-maximization algorithm or by direct maximization of the observed-data likelihood with Fisher scoring; standard errors are available via observed or expected information. When total exposure is common to all subjects, a relative slope summarizes the treatment effect and, unlike the rate ratio, does not depend on the assumed total exposure. In simulations, interval coverage was near nominal when enough events occurred during each treatment condition. The models are implemented in the R package maskcave. The work was motivated by the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study of 10,948 children. Assuming 16 waking hours per day, the adjusted sport-to-non-sport rate ratio for mild traumatic brain injury was 8.78 (95% confidence interval 4.47-17.27). We applied the count model to concussions during sports reported for 6,379 children at the Year 5 visit: the concussion rate per hour of football was 2.46 (1.37-4.43) times that of the other reported sports.

title: Multicollinearity diagnosis in generalized linear models: A systematic review and empirical reassessment
abstract: Ridge-type estimators are widely used to address multicollinearity in generalized linear models (GLMs), yet their empirical justification depends heavily on how multicollinearity is diagnosed. Following systematic review guidelines, we conduct a citation-based review of 120 real-data applications to examine current diagnostic practices. The findings reveal a lack of consensus across studies: approaches vary regarding data transformation prior to diagnosis, applying transformations to either the design matrix or the weighted information matrix, while others omit transformation entirely. Nevertheless, the condition number emerges as the most widely used diagnostic. We review existing methodologies for computing the condition number in GLMs and recommend the optimal approach, as it uniquely attains its minimum value under orthogonality while retaining the intercept. Finally, these formulations are implemented in R and used to replicate five real-data applications from the literature.

title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
abstract: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information. In a competitive market with resource-constrained forecasting, more capable algorithms can substitute analysis of public records for private observations, reducing the private information aggregated into prices. The same trades can convey sophisticated public-data analysis to investors unable to perform it themselves. We establish conditions under which these effects coexist and the private benefit of further computation falls. Numerical equilibrium calculations and finite-data neural-market experiments exhibit corresponding patterns. Out-of-sample earnings forecasts and controlled language-model tasks show related patterns of information substitution. In the neural experiment, wider adoption increases the predictive value of price for limited observers, reduces it for advanced observers, and lowers the benefit of upgrading by 44\%. Retraining by investors who did not upgrade can amplify the loss of private-information precision. The informational consequences of AI trading depend on what prices reveal and who can use them.

title: Functional nestedness of soil nematode communities across Europe: integrating morphological counts and eDNA reads
abstract: 1. Soil nematodes occupy multiple trophic positions and contribute to key processes in soil food webs. Their communities vary across land uses and environmental conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these differences mainly reflect taxon replacement or nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 2. Here, we analysed two independent European datasets of soil nematode communities, SOB4ES, based on eDNA metabarcoding, and NemEu, based on morphological identification, to examine how genus composition varies across land uses. We partitioned community dissimilarity into turnover and nestedness-resultant components and compared sites under contrasting land uses with those sharing the same land use, while accounting for geographical and soil-related variation. We also assessed matrix-level nestedness, differences among trophic groups and associations between genus composition and environmental gradients. 3. In both datasets, genus turnover was consistently greater between contrasting land uses than within the same land use. Although the differences were modest, they remained significant after accounting for geographical distance and genus richness, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity contributed little to land-use differentiation. These findings suggest that land-use-associated differences in European nematode communities are expressed primarily through changes in genus identity rather than nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 4. The consistency of this result across independently assembled datasets supports the broader relevance of taxonomic turnover for understanding soil biodiversity patterns across European land uses.

title: Estimating a Rational Inattention Discrete Choice Model: A Semiparametric Approach
abstract: People's choices depend on both the payoffs of the available options and what they learn about those payoffs before deciding. This paper shows how choice data identify both unobserved payoff heterogeneity and the cost of information acquisition in a rational inattention discrete-choice model. I establish conditions for semiparametric point identification using exogenous payoff and information-cost shifters, without imposing parametric forms on the taste-shock distribution or on how the unit cost of information varies with observed characteristics. In the model with binary choice, I construct an unobserved choice threshold whose cumulative distribution function is the choice probability as a function of the payoff shifter. Moments of this threshold identify the payoff coefficients and the unit cost of information at each value of the information-cost shifter. A deconvolution argument then identifies the taste-shock distribution. I then extend identification to the model with multinomial choice. To estimate the model, I propose a sieve minimum-distance estimator based on observed market shares and establish its consistency. For inference, I construct confidence regions by test inversion because binding parameter constraints can make the estimator's limiting distribution nonnormal. In an application to Amazon Mechanical Turk, model counterfactuals show that lower unit costs of information raise the average task-taking probability and reduce wage elasticity.

title: Stochastic Games with Distributional Entropy Objectives
abstract: We introduce \emph{stochastic games with distributional entropy objectives}, two-player zero-sum games whose configurations are probability distributions over the states of a finite arena and whose stage reward is Shannon entropy. Over an infinite discounted horizon, MIN seeks to concentrate the distribution, while MAX seeks to disperse it. Because entropy is nonlinear, it matters whether strategic and transition randomness are averaged before entropy is evaluated or sampled first. We formalise three resulting semantics: averaged-distribution, sampled-profile, and sampled-transition. This semantic choice fundamentally changes the game-theoretic structure. Averaged-distribution games need not be determined, even on a four-state deterministic arena, whereas both sampled semantics are determined and admit optimal stationary randomised strategies. We give contractive Bellman characterisations and convergent finite-horizon approximations for the upper and lower averaged values and the two sampled values. Moreover, even the lower value under averaged-distribution semantics dominates the value under either sampled semantics, while the sampled-profile and sampled-transition values are incomparable in general. For fixed rational discount and positive rational promise gap, the averaged-distribution (upper and lower value) gap problems and both sampled gap problems lie in PSPACE; for a single entropy minimiser, the averaged and sampled-profile problems lie in NP. Finally, under all three semantics, entropy optimisation is NP-hard to approximate within a suitable fixed additive constant, already for deterministic one-player games, where pure memoryless strategies are optimal.

title: Disenfranchisement in Spatial Voting Games
abstract: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.

title: Dynamic bigraphical Mat\'ern--Whittle processes: learning dependence graphs among spatial-temporal fields
abstract: Many studies record several variables at the same sites over a sequence of periods, such as pollutant concentrations at monitoring stations or case counts of infectious diseases by district. A central question concerns the dependence between the variables and its change over time. We develop dynamic bigraphical Mat\'ern--Whittle (DBMW) processes for such data. Each variable has a spatial field that evolves by autoregression. A graph over the variables couples the temporal innovations of the fields. Its links appear and vanish over time, and a link may change sign. A graph Laplacian on the sites gives the spatial structure, and a canonical exponential family links the fields to Gaussian, count or binomial responses. The joint distribution of the latent fields over all sites, variables and periods factorizes over the eigenmodes of the graph Laplacian, and its normalizing constant is free of the graph and of the dynamics. Given the fields, the posterior of the time-varying signed graph is therefore exact, by forward--backward recursions. The estimator has three steps: a fit without a graph, which also gives the switching rates with an interval, the exact graph posterior, and a joint refit. In simulations, DBMW recovers the graph with higher average precision than graphical lasso, time-varying graphical lasso and Poisson log-normal networks, and it predicts withheld data better than a standard spatio-temporal model that fits each variable separately, with a Mat\'ern field and autoregressive evolution, by integrated nested Laplace approximation. In weekly air-quality data from 288 U.S. sites, it recovers the seasonal change of sign between ozone and nitrogen dioxide. In German surveillance data on seven diseases, the district-level links stay positive and stable through the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Hidden Markov Models for Dynamic Co-Clustering
abstract: To jointly identify temporal regimes and row-column structure in matrix-valued time series, we propose a hidden Markov model (HMM) with Gaussian co-clustering distributions. A single latent regime governs each matrix. Conditional on the regime, row and column memberships define Gaussian blocks, each with its own mean and variance. Membership probabilities and block parameters are shared across occurrences of a regime, while individual memberships may vary between time points.

title: Constrained Stochastic Policy Targeting under Heterogeneous Partial Interference
abstract: Under heterogeneous interference, treating individuals with particular characteristics affects the population average outcome through their heterogeneous direct response to treatment and indirect effect on others, creating opportunities for efficient policy design. For instance, policymakers may minimize resource use by vaccinating individuals identified as superspreaders to achieve a target reduction in disease incidence. In such setting, we first study the problem of learning individualized stochastic treatment policies that minimize population average treatment probability subject to a prespecified outcome target. We propose an estimation approach based on a smooth surrogate for constraint violations and interference-aware inverse-probability-weighting or self-normalized estimators of the population average outcome, and establish finite-sample regret guarantees for both estimators. We also consider the complementary problem of maximizing the population average outcome subject to a constraint on average treatment probability. We apply the proposed methodology to a Colombian conditional cash transfer program aimed at improving school attendance. The application demonstrates that accounting for interference and individualizing treatment probabilities can reduce resource use relative to policies that ignore interference or impose homogeneous treatment probabilities.

title: Causal Regularization for Robust Prediction
abstract: Prediction is an important use of a statistical model. However, predictive systems typically struggle when the environment, in which they were trained, changes. Robust prediction that can deal with distributional shifts has become an active research area. Existing approaches tend to make strong assumptions in order to achieve prediction guarantees. In this paper, we only require finite second moments in the training data to obtain sharp prediction guarantees. We generalize causal regularization to a framework that uses two environments and measures the differences between them through a generalized risk difference induced by changes in second-order moments of the covariates and response. By defining a sieve of out-of-sample distributions, we derive a worst-risk decomposition over increasing classes of environments and obtain a closed-form estimator that interpolates between OLS and the regularization limit solution. Causal interpretation is recovered under the inner-product invariance condition and when the conditional mean of the target given its causal parents remains invariant across environments. Our results show that the proposed estimator can achieve prediction stability over a broad class of perturbed environments, even when trained on a limited set. The framework separates two goals: robustness as a stable prediction under weak assumptions and causality as a stronger property obtained with additional invariance structure.

title: A fast and sound algorithm to simplify summations in interventional queries expressions
abstract: Identification formulas returned by the ID algorithm often contain summations that can be removed. The procedure proposed in arxiv:1806.07082 (TK) removes them by combining factors of the formula into joint distributions, through the chain rule and through the insertion of factors for missing variables. We make two changes to this procedure: only the factors that involve the summed variable are combined, and every factor is written with a minimal conditioning set. These two changes determine the rest of the procedure, in which each search over a power set is replaced by a single test and the variables to insert are fixed in advance, and they remove summations that the TK procedure leaves in place. The resulting procedure is sound and, for minimal input terms, complete for each individual elimination with respect to joins and insertions.

title: Making Experiment Results Comparable through Sitewide Impact Estimation
abstract: Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this experiment lift is not comparable across surfaces, because surfaces differ in reach and in their contribution to sitewide metrics. The quantity a strategic decision needs is a counterfactual-how much an aggregated sitewide metric (e.g., total platform play time) would move if the treatment reached 100% of its target population, which may be only part of the sitewide population, during the measurement period. We call this sitewide impact. Its scaling factor, which we call the coverage factor, combines the reach and the target population's contribution to the sitewide metric under no treatment. Hence a low-reach surface whose users carry much of the metric could outrank a high-reach surface whose users carry little. We develop two estimators under this framing: one for difference-in-means metrics and one for variant-level ratio metrics (a metric defined as a ratio of two population aggregates). Empirically, experiment lift is a poor proxy for sitewide impact-across 139 experiments that are statistically significant on time spent, the Spearman rank correlation between the two is 0.20, and 5 of the 10 largest experiment lifts are among the 10 largest sitewide impacts. We validate the estimator with A/A tests and against a long-term holdout, and apply it to cross-domain prioritization and attributing year-over-year growth to shipped innovations.

title: Comments on: `CliPS: How to identify cluster distributions in Bayesian mixture models'
abstract: I congratulate the authors on their contribution, which addresses important challenges in understanding posterior distributions in Bayesian mixture models. As underlined by the authors, the Bayesian framework has several advantages, yet label-switching, identifiability issues, and the trans-dimensional nature of parameter spaces make exploiting the Bayesian approach and understanding the resulting posterior difficult in practice. The paper offers clear explanations and a simple, intuitive procedure to address this by clustering the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws of component-specific parameters. It is clearly illustrated on several examples.

title: Asymptotic properties for weak Markov-switching AR(p) models
abstract: In this paper we study the asymptotic properties of an autoregressive model of order p (AR for short), possibly non-centered, whose parameters switch according to an unobserved Markov chain. Departing from the conventional assumption of independent innovations, we merely require the errors to be uncorrelated but not necessarily independent, thereby widening substantially the range of potential applications of Markov-switching AR models. We establish sufficient conditions for the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed moment estimators. We also propose a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance matrix of the moment estimators. The finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures is illustrated through Monte Carlo experiments and an empirical study based on hourly meteorological data, which together provide strong support for the theoretical findings.

title: The Algebra of Narratives and the Monitoring of Their Relative Dominance
abstract: We propose an algebraic methodology for measuring the relative prevalence of competing narratives within a time-evolving corpus of texts. Standard cosine similarity between article embedding and narrative vectors fails to isolate the idiosyncratic contribution of each narrative, because narratives sharing a common topic produce strongly correlated vector representations. We address this by orthogonalizing the narrative vectors via a global max-min optimization on the Stiefel manifold, which neutralizes shared semantic components while preserving each narrative's specific direction. We ground this geometric procedure in a linear generative model for article embedding that provides an unbiased estimator of narrative prevalence and formally explains why the naive approach suffers from a correlation bias. Empirical validation on the publicly available News Category Dataset (Huff Post, 2012-2018) confirms that the orthogonalized estimator recovers narrative-specific dynamics aligned with known historical events, whereas the naive cosine projection yields synchronized, uninformative time series.

title: Quantifying Dependence Effects on $k$-out-of-$n$ Reliability Relative to the Independent Benchmark
abstract: Understanding how dependence among component lifetimes affects the reliability of redundant systems is a central problem in reliability engineering. In this paper, we develop a framework for quantifying the impact of multivariate dependence on $k$-out-of-$n$ system reliability relative to the independent benchmark. Using an orthogonal Legendre expansion of the copula density, we derive an exact decomposition that separates the dependence structure from the system architecture. This representation identifies how individual dependence contributions are transmitted to system reliability through explicit structural weights. An application to multivariate Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern copulas demonstrates that higher-order dependence can produce distinct reliability effects even when all bivariate copulas remain unchanged. Our findings provide a systematic approach to quantifying and interpreting the effects of multivariate dependence on the reliability of redundant systems.

title: Exploitation, class income and welfare in a Sraffian economy with consumption preferences
abstract: This paper develops a Sraffian model of simple reproduction in which production prices and functional income distribution remain classically determined, while class consumption is chosen optimally at those prices and incomes. it then shows that once workers and capitalists choose consumption bundles according to class-specific preferences, rather than consuming fixed baskets, surplus value, exploitation rates, total profits, and capitalist welfare need not rise monotonically with the profit rate. The framework defines distributive Engel curves, tracing how consumption, profits, labor exploitation, and welfare vary along the wage-profit frontier. Higher profitability may expand capitalists' nominal claim on surplus, yet alter relative prices in ways that reduce their real consumption and welfare. The result qualifies standard Marxian and Sraffian accounts of net product distribution based on the wage-profit curve.

title: Who sees the sea? Sea-view potential by fa\c{c}ade and floor from cadastral LoD1 models on the Costa del Sol
abstract: Views are among the most valued and least measured attributes of a home. We present an open-data method that estimates the sea-view potential of every free fa\c{c}ade of every residential building at three floors (ground, middle and top; other floors take the nearest of them), from cadastral footprints with floor counts and a national terrain model. Run for 158,060 buildings of 21 municipalities on Spain's Costa del Sol in under an hour on two cores, it finds that 52 % of buildings see some sea from their top floor and 36 % have an open view (20{\deg} or more). Traced over a LiDAR surface in a pilot, scores agree with the model's inside cadastral footprints (96.7 % of viewpoints in the same class at 20{\deg}), but structures the cadastre does not record lower the sea seen from the top floor by 6.1--9.0{\deg} on average. Against the photographs of 93 homes for sale, labelled blind by AI models of two developers with ties decided by the author, the score has an AUC of 0.80 (95 % CI 0.70--0.89; 0.81 against the first-round labels); at 20{\deg} it is sensitive (0.90) but not specific (0.45). Dwelling figures depend on how dwellings are allocated to fa\c{c}ades and floors: 42 % of dwellings are on a floor with open-view potential under the main rule, and 12--45 % across the allocation, geometry and vegetation scenarios tested. As an application, higher-income census sections tend to have more modelled view potential within municipalities, with uncertain size and fragile inference (about two effective clusters); on terrain alone the difference largely disappears. Code and fa\c{c}ade-level data reproduce the main results.

title: Identification and Inference of Bi-directional Causal Effects in Mendelian Randomization without Instrument Selection
abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects. Bidirectional MR usually uses two reversed unidirectional analyses, but feedback can invalidate instruments in at least one direction and induce correlated pleiotropy. We model both traits as a stable cyclic system and estimate both directional effects from GWAS summary data without instrument selection or a prespecified valid-instrument subset. After LD score normalisation, marginal associations form a heteroscedastic noisy independent component analysis model, assuming the variants' direct effects on the two traits are independent. If those effects are non-Gaussian, this identifies the total-effect matrix up to scaling and permutation; no-self-feedback and stability of the system further resolve these ambiguities. We develop an estimator based on noise-adjusted second- and fourth-order moments, avoiding inversion of the high-dimensional linkage disequilibrium matrix and having computational cost linear in the number of variants. Under weak local dependence, we establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and validity of a chromosome-respecting moving block bootstrap. Simulations show negligible bias, generally reliable interval coverage, and higher rejection rates for nonzero directional effects than focusing-based tests. Three real-data applications illustrate how joint analysis of feedback systems can yield causal decompositions differing from two separate unidirectional analyses.

title: Safe manipulation of tops-only voting rules
abstract: We study tops-only voting rules on the domain of all preferences with a unique top, focusing on manipulation by risk-avoiding voters. Following Hartman et al.(2025), we measure resistance to manipulation by the RAT-degree: the minimum number of other voters' reports that a voter needs to observe for a ``safe'' manipulation to become possible. Given the observed reports, such a manipulation weakly improves on truthful reporting under every completion of the unobserved reports and strictly improves on it under at least one completion. For any finite set of at least three alternatives, we show that anonymity, unanimity, and winner monotonicity imply an upper bound of $\lceil n/2\rceil$ on the RAT-degree, where $n$ is the number of voters. We provide exact characterizations of the RAT-degree for anonymous generalized median voter schemes and voting by quotas, without imposing single-peakedness or separability on preferences. For odd $n$, the median voter rule and objectwise majority rule uniquely maximize the RAT-degree within their respective classes and attain the general upper bound.

title: Extended Bayesian Estimation for In-flight Calibration of Space-based Instruments
authors: Soham Das and Yang Chen and David A. van Dyk and Herman L. Marshall and Vinay L. Kashyap and Michael Smith
abstract: The ongoing calibration of space-based instruments is essential to ensure accurate measurements of physical quantities such as photon flux. The goal is to obtain a unified photon-flux measurement of a single astronomical source using data obtained with multiple instruments. Calibration involves in-flight adjustments to address discrepancies arising from instrument-specific variations. Taking a statistical approach, we extend a previously proposed additive log-Normal hierarchical model with half-variance correction based on a multiplicative physical model for photon counts. The newly proposed Bayesian hierarchical model can leverage domain-specific priors to account for correlated passbands and integrate information across different instruments, sources, and passbands effectively. The model is fitted using Markov chain Monte Carlo and can provide uncertainty quantification for instrument- and source-specific parameter estimation. Moreover, we obtain valid inferences for other structural parameters of the physics model. We use data derived from Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray observatories to illustrate the proposed inference procedure.

title: Broken Adaptive Ridge in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressions
abstract: We study regularized estimation in high-dimensional vector autoregressions under physical dependence and row-wise approximate sparsity using the Broken Adaptive Ridge (BAR) estimator. BAR is an iteratively reweighted Ridge procedure whose fixed-point first-order conditions imply a coordinatewise thresholding rule that produces exact zeros. We show that the BAR estimation error can be analyzed on the union of the population support above the BAR threshold and the support selected in the sample. The size of this union can be controlled at the rate implied by approximate sparsity, allowing us to establish the required restricted-curvature condition and derive L1, L2, and prediction error rates when the number of regressors grows polynomially with the sample size and may exceed it. Under exact sparsity, the resulting rates recover the familiar rates for sparse high-dimensional estimation. Monte Carlo experiments across a range of high-dimensional VAR designs show that BAR delivers strong estimation and forecasting performance, and retains a high share of relevant coefficients relative to Lasso, adaptive Lasso, and SCAD. An application to U.S. inflation forecasting using FRED-MD shows particularly strong performance at the one-month horizon.

title: Causal and conditional tail coefficients: asymptotics, inference and graph recovery
abstract: The causal tail coefficient (CTC) measures the influence of an extreme value of one variable on another variable and has been proposed as a tool for causal discovery in heavy-tailed models. Despite its popularity, the asymptotic behavior of its empirical counterpart has not been well understood. We develop an asymptotic theory for the rank-based CTC estimator with an intermediate threshold under nonparametric conditions that are satisfied by all standard copula models. A key observation is that the CTC is determined by the mean of a conditional tail limit distribution, which clarifies its interpretation and determines the asymptotic variance of the estimator. We establish joint asymptotic normality for the entire CTC matrix and prove consistency of a multiplier bootstrap for simultaneous inference. For heavy-tailed linear and recursive max-linear structural equation models, we show that the CTC equals one if and only if the first variable is an ancestor of the second, which leads to confidence graphs for the ancestral graph with asymptotic coverage guarantees. All results extend to general conditional tail coefficients, defined as further functionals of the conditional tail limit distribution. A simulation study and an application to dietary intake data illustrate the methods.

title: Go under Chinese Rules with a Succinct Game History is Complete for Exponential Space
abstract: The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play. Many games, such as Hex or Othello, are PSPACE-complete: the game tree has polynomial depth, so the game can be decided in PSPACE. However, some games allow exponentially long plays, for instance Chess (without a generalized 50-move rule) or Go under Japanese rules; these are complete for exponential time. To prevent infinite games, some games employ a no-repetition rule (super-ko rule), for instance Go under Chinese rules. Robson (1984) proved that Chess and Checkers with a no-repetition rule are even harder: deciding whether the first player has a winning strategy is EXPSPACE-complete. Since then, it has been an open problem whether Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete, too. The complexity of a game under a no-repetition rule is typically interpreted as follows: given a board position, decide whether the first player has a winning strategy such that no repetition occurs from that position on. We introduce the concept of a succinct game history: a Boolean circuit that, given a board position, outputs 1 if the position is in the game history and 0 otherwise. It serves as a "judge" that tells the players whether a move is illegal because it creates a repetition. We prove that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly. Moreover, the starting position in our hardness proof is reachable by legal gameplay, which has not always been the case in prior proofs.

title: A Bayesian approach to technological emergence, climate variability, and demographic stability in northern South America
abstract: Human communities produce technology in almost every environment, but the conditions that enable technologies in the tropics are not well understood. We test two competing hypotheses---that technological emergence is triggered by environmental stress and that technology tracks growth in effective populations---by integrating Holocene archaeological and paleoclimate evidence. We use archaeological derived radiocarbon dates from Colombia as a proxy for human activity, including dating plant management, pottery, metallurgy, and raised fields. For palaeoclimate, we use two El Ni\~no--Southern Oscillation (ENSO) reconstructions: Laguna Pallcacocha and Laguna El Junco in Ecuador. A Bayesian changepoint at 3575 cal BP (95% highest posterior density interval (HPDI) = 3811--3329) marks a ~13-fold increase in the growth rate of pre-Hispanic human activity ($r_2$/$r_1$ median = 13.3, 95% HPDI = 8.1--22.2). Plant management and pottery predate this shift by more than a millennium, whereas metallurgy and raised fields cluster within the early acceleration phase, during relative climatic and demographic stability. A Bayesian log-linear regression of human activity on ENSO frequency and intensity after the demographic changepoint reveals an asymmetric covariation: reduced ENSO frequency and intensity suppress activity by 58% and 21%, whereas ENSO frequency raises activity modestly (~11--13%). Therefore, ENSO regulates demographic activity rather than triggering technological emergence. These patterns suggest that pre-Columbian communities may have innovated when they could compute---when an effective population sat above a critical threshold and stability windows permitted combinatorial search---rather than when they were forced to by environmental stress, expressed as demographic or climatic variability.

title: LaMe: a Joint Latent Mediation Framework for High-Dimensional Systems
abstract: Mediation analysis seeks to understand how an exposure influences an outcome through intermediate variables. However, as increasingly rich datasets become available, hundreds to thousands of potential mediators make these systems difficult to model and hard to interpret. Latent-variable approaches offer a natural way to accommodate these high-dimensional settings. However, existing latent mediation methods face limitations, including overparameterization, biased inference, or limited scalability. We develop LaMe, a joint linear-Gaussian framework that summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system through a small number of latent variables. We identify natural direct and indirect effects under an explicit assumption that the manifest measurements fully capture the latent mediators, and characterize conditions under which the latent representation effectively restricts the observed cross-covariance structure. Simulations assess recovery of observed association parameters, natural effects, and manifest features associated with latent mediation pathways across a range of challenging settings. Four real-world applications demonstrate competitive predictive performance with compact latent representations, including single-dimensional representations of biomarker and proteomic measurements. Together, these results establish LaMe as a practical framework for estimating and summarizing multivariate mediation systems under explicit structural and measurement assumptions.

title: Characterizing M-estimators using canonical divergences from information geometry
abstract: On Euclidean space, the losses that produce consistent M-estimators of a functional are its strictly consistent scoring functions (Dimitriadis, Fissler and Ziegel, 2024), and Osband's principle characterizes these through identification functions, which define method-of-moments estimators. We extend this characterization to the probability simplex. We define the residual, which on Euclidean space is a subtraction, as the inverse exponential map of an affine connection. It identifies the exponential barycenter of the connection: the arithmetic, normalized geometric and Fr\'echet means for the mixture, exponential and Levi-Civita connections. Its integral along geodesics is the canonical divergence of Ay and Amari (2015). A geometric form of Osband's principle decides which losses each connection admits. For the flat connections every strictly convex generator yields a consistent Bregman loss. For the curved $\alpha$-connections, half the squared Fisher-Rao distance is (up to scale) the only consistent loss for the Fr\'echet mean, and for $\alpha \notin \{-1, 0, 1\}$ no such loss exists and only the method of moments remains. The residual is integrable only at $\alpha = 0$, sharpening the integrability claim of Ay and Amari. The characterization yields the estimating equations of regression on the simplex and the calibration decomposition of compositional forecasts.

title: Cross-Fitted Doubly Robust Estimation with Student-t Outcome Engines: ECM Algorithms, Monte Carlo Evidence and Schistosomiasis Programme Data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo
authors: Cosmas Kambale Musambi and Ernest Fokou\'e
abstract: Routine data on preventive chemotherapy for schistosomiasis are confounded, clustered, heavy-tailed and heaped. We study how cross-fitted augmented inverse probability weighted (AIPW) estimators behave, and how they should be computed, when least squares is replaced by Student-t outcome engines: Huber and t iteratively reweighted least squares, and a two-component t scale-mixture regression fitted by an ECM algorithm, alongside a residual-clipped augmentation. We give four short propositions (exact AIPW bias, the efficiency bound, the estimand of clipping, monotone ascent of a scale-constrained ECM), a single-file Python implementation with cluster-level cross-fitting, cluster-robust standard errors and a cluster bootstrap, and a Monte Carlo study with up to 1000 replications per cell. Robust outcome engines leave AIPW unchanged (RMSE differences at most 0.002), whereas clipping cuts RMSE by 26-45% under symmetric contamination, under-covers, and, as a plasmode experiment built on real covariates and residuals shows, shifts the estimand when residual laws differ between arms. One-sided artefacts that differ between arms bias every estimator. Heaped data also break naive code: the MAD scale collapses and the mixture likelihood is unbounded, and we give simple guards. Applied to 1485 rounds in 362 health zones of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (ESPEN, 2014-2025), integrated delivery appears to raise programme coverage by 17.4 percentage points, yet epidemiological coverage differs by only 0.9: the gap comes from targeting denominators, a real differential artefact that no outcome engine can remove.

title: Positive Weights Do Not Certify TWFE Inference: A Design Diagnostic under Treatment-Effect Heterogeneity
abstract: Conventional two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) inference need not be uniformly adequate even when all treatment weights are positive. Under a local treatment-effect drift, the statistic for the equally weighted treated-cell effect has worst-case mean shift $(c/q)\Gamma$, where $\Gamma=\sqrt{N_1}\|w-u\|_2$ is design-only and $q$ is the cluster-score noise scale. Projection matches the exposure to cohort, event-time, additive, and saturated group-time pilots; when residualized treatment is constant within treated group-time cells, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{gt}}=\Gamma$. A direct score estimator is feasible with fixed panel length as clusters grow. Because a debiased quadratic pilot is nonregular at zero, we use two regular one-sided procedures: a reverse-triangle multiplier lower bound to detect unsafe envelopes and covariance-aware noncentral-$\chi^2$ inversion to certify adequacy. At $5\%$ nominal size with a five-point tolerance, the shift threshold is $0.652$. In the Callaway--Sant'Anna minimum-wage panel, where every treated-cell weight is positive, the saturated $95\%$ lower shift bound is $0.793$, so conventional inference is not uniformly certified. A complementary Brazilian property-tax reanalysis with $2{,}840$ municipalities withholds certification in all four classes; its smallest lower bound is $1.040$. Under the maintained many-cluster approximation, castle-doctrine homicide passes for additive cohort-plus-event-time heterogeneity with a $95\%$ upper bound of $0.236$; its saturated covariance lacks one required rank. Divorce is inconclusive. These envelopes are not predictions of realized rejection. The diagnostic separates point correction, uniform exposure, and statistically warranted certification.

title: Does Increasing Government Spending on Tertiary Education Provide a Return on Investment? A Bayesian Causal Inference Analysis
abstract: When a government increases public spending on tertiary (university) education, does it provide a positive fiscal return on investment once general economic growth is separated out? Cross-country data make this hard to answer because growing economies naturally collect more tax, international ratios divide per-student spending by GDP per person and student headcount, and cohorts take years to graduate. We assemble a five-year panel of 121 countries (1985-2024) and fit continuous-treatment Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests that model four tax changes jointly whilst adjusting for starting conditions, predicted funding, and follow-up economic growth. A +10 percentage-point (pp) increase in per-student university spending (% of GDP per person) shifts the tax mix toward direct income and profit taxation by +0.36 pp after 5 years (93% probability of a positive effect) and +0.71 pp after 10 years (96% probability). Overall tax-to-GDP takes a decade to respond as cohorts graduate: 10-year total non-resource tax rises by +0.24 pp of GDP (89% probability) and direct income tax by +0.12 pp (90% probability) per +10 pp of per-student spending, by +0.37 pp (100% probability) after five-year within-country funding increases, and by +0.22 pp in total tax (95% probability) and +0.15 pp in direct income tax (98% probability) per +25% increase in real PPP dollars per student. Comparing one entering cohort's degree cost against its 40-year career tax payments shows a typical three- to five-fold total tax return in high-income economies (EUR 2.37 billion in Ireland returning EUR 9.66 billion in total tax with a 77% probability of net profit and EUR 2.87 billion in direct income tax, or EUR 11.55 billion in the UK returning EUR 58.33 billion), whereas expanding the university budget without protecting spending per student yields no return.

title: Endogenous Parcel Contiguity and Rent Indeterminacy in a Finite-Household Monocentric City
abstract: We study a monocentric city with finitely many households, each of which may hold any measurable set of land and incurs commuting costs that depend on the spatial distribution of its holdings. In equilibrium, every parcel is an interval and parcels are ordered by lot size from the center outward. The freedom to adjust land holdings at any location restricts supporting rents to a band between the competing bid rents and the assigned household's bid rent. This band excludes rents that support the same allocation when lots are restricted to intervals, including the one constructed by Berliant and Fujita (1992), and makes the existence of a supporting rent a substantive question even with identical households. We give sufficient conditions for the existence of a locally supporting rent that meets every household's budget and deters all small deviations. We also show that any equilibrium minimizes the real resource cost of attaining equilibrium utilities and extend the sorting result to heterogeneous households under a single-crossing condition. Finally, we discuss the relation to hedonic models, distinguishing the prices of whole parcels from location-specific rents that govern the cost of changes in parcel boundaries and fragmentation.

title: evgmrf: An R Package For Gaussian Markov Random Field Extreme Value Models
authors: Benjamin D. Youngman and Ayu Shabrina
abstract: We introduce \textsf{evgmrf}, an \textsf{R} package for fitting spatially varying extreme value models using Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRFs). The package supports the generalized extreme value distribution for block maxima, the generalized Pareto distribution for threshold exceedances, the Poisson--GPD point-process model, and the $r$-largest order-statistics model. Distributional parameters may vary over regular spatial grids or arbitrary regions that can be represented by a valid adjacency matrix, with optional fixed effects and covariate dependence. Spatial structure is represented through intrinsic conditional autoregressive, proper conditional autoregressive, and Besag--York--Molli\'{e} 2 models, which are extended with non-Gaussian random-effect distributions. Estimation uses penalized likelihood with smoothing or dependence hyper-parameters estimated using a Laplace approximation, exploiting sparse precision matrices for computational efficiency. The package provides methods for model summaries, spatial visualization, prediction on link and response scales, estimation of extreme quantiles, and uncertainty quantification in the form of approximate standard error estimates, or via simulations from parameter sampling distributions. Examples based on gridded and county-level precipitation data illustrate the use of the package for spatial modelling of environmental extremes. \textsf{evgmrf} provides a unified, accessible framework for extreme value analyses in which distributional parameters exhibit structured spatial variation.

title: Menu Design Meets Market Design: Strategic Simplicity vs. Choice Complexity
abstract: Strategic simplicity removes the incentive to misreport preferences, but it does not ensure that participants can identify what they prefer. We study this distinction in a laboratory experiment on serial dictatorships, where optimal play only requires choosing one's favorite bundle of real-effort tasks. Participants make fifteen incentivized choices among bundles that vary in how many tasks they combine. They choose either from a large menu or through a series of binary choices. Having made all choices, they unexpectedly reconsider each assignment against a previously rejected alternative. We find that roughly one in six choices is reversed and almost one in five involves an objectively dominated bundle. Simplifying the choice architecture does not help. Binary decomposition even raises reversal rates among low-ability participants and further inflates their confidence about their choices.

title: Efficient and Practical Clustering of Variables in Causal Graphs
abstract: Clustering variables in a graph may improve visual clarity and simplify causal inference. Harnessing the full potential of clustering requires an automated method to detect useful clusters in a graph. We introduce a novel class of clusters called conduits, and present a sound, complete and efficient algorithm for detecting all conduits in the graph. In addition to algorithmic detectability, conduits appear naturally in causal graphs stemming from real-world applications, enabling substantial size reduction. Furthermore, the structure of conduits enables the application of known identifiability results regarding clustering. We demonstrate these properties in a simulation study with real-world graphs.

title: Stratified Randomization Incorporating Historical Control Data
abstract: Randomized controlled trials are often infeasible in rare diseases because of limited sample size, high costs, or lengthy durations. Hybrid control designs address this by combining a concurrent control arm with historical data. However, existing methods such as propensity score matching (PSM) borrow historical data only at the analysis stage, which limits power gains when covariate distributions differ between historical and concurrent data. We propose a stratified block randomization method for hybrid control trials. Within each stratum, more concurrent subjects are allocated to the treatment arm than to the concurrent control arm, and the difference is filled with historical controls so that the treatment and hybrid control arms are balanced 1:1; once the available historical controls in the stratum are used or a pre-specified overall cap is reached, allocation returns to 1:1. Historical controls are incorporated either by sampling or by weighting. We compared both methods with PSM in terms of type I error rate, power, and sample size via Monte Carlo simulations. The sampling method maintained the type I error rates when there was neither heterogeneity in the outcome model nor unmeasured covariates. It also had power comparable to or greater than that of PSM, particularly when historical controls were unevenly distributed across strata. The power of the weighting method increased with the pooled historical sample size, but its type I error rate was inflated when covariates beyond the stratification factors were present or when stratification factors were dichotomized from continuous covariates. The proposed method incorporates historical data at the allocation stage rather than only at the analysis stage, enabling more efficient use of historical data.

title: A Consistent Bayesian Adaptive Quotient Graph Framework for Graph-Informed Random Partition Models
authors: Kun Huang and Xiyu Peng and Huiyan Sang
abstract: Bayesian graph-informed random partition models are widely used to model heterogeneity in structured data. A prominent approach assigns a prior directly on the space of contiguous partitions of a pre-determined graph G; however, such models are not data-adaptive and can be computationally infeasible for large graphs. To address these limitations, we propose a Bayesian adaptive quotient graph framework that induces partitions through a two-level hierarchical prior: a prior is first imposed on quotient graphs of G, followed by a conditional prior on a reduced contiguous partition space induced by each quotient graph. We develop high-level assumptions that guide the construction of the two-level prior such that the reduced space retains desirable partitions. We further establish high-level assumptions for posterior concentration on desirable quotient graphs and partitions. The framework can be readily embedded into many existing Bayesian hierarchical models with latent cluster structures as a contiguous random partition prior. As a specific example, we apply the proposed framework to the spatial random partition model proposed in Huang and Sang (2026). The resulting model adapts to the unknown number of clusters, achieves a faster clustering-consistency contraction rate, and yields substantially lower partition error and computation time in simulations. Finally, we apply the resulting model to a large spatial transcriptomics dataset to demonstrate its practical utility.

title: Estimand-specific bootstrap confidence intervals after optimism correction for prediction models
abstract: Confidence intervals after bootstrap optimism correction are often reported for prediction models, but what they cover depends on the estimand. We distinguish two estimands: the target-population performance of the final model developed from the observed sample, $\theta_{\mathrm{FM},n}$, and the average performance over repeated model development, $\theta_{\mathrm{proc},n}$. Using first-order expansions of the estimation errors, we identify the bootstrap root that matches the error for $\theta_{\mathrm{FM},n}$.
