title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
abstract: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.

title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.

title: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text
abstract: We study AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a monetary total, and the human readings that anchor the machines disagree. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings (799,675 records, \$126.4B), labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with a designed sample of 651 texts read independently by three people under one codebook. We state exact conditions for a fixed-predictor difference estimator and for a cross-fitted predictor whose folds are assigned to the whole frame before sampling, under Poisson sampling, and assess the implemented fixed-size procedures by simulation: 8 predictors whose own totals span \$11.2-15.0B agree to within \$0.4B once rectified. Two rules that accept machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, weighted conformal p-values under a dollar measure and Learn-then-Test on the design estimate of the error, are evaluated on nested held-out folds and on re-draws of the design with synthetic truths; their error control in deployment is not established, and the count-based rule accepts no text under a dollar-drawn sample. In a replay that charges every human label, a two-phase review policy whose calibrator is fitted on its own first phase reduces the RMSE of the total by 28% at a budget of 100 texts relative to dollar-proportional sampling, while pure Neyman allocation fails with an uncalibrated predictor. Independent readers shift the estimated total by \$3.93B, 2.2 times the within-reader sampling interval, and institution-level intervals under-cover at every size. Every headline result is re-run under each reader. The results identify both the benefits and the limits of using learned predictions to decide what a person should verify.

title: Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
abstract: GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.

title: Ratio-of-mediator-probability weighting for causal mediation analysis: estimation, extensions, and practical guidance
abstract: Ratio-of-mediator-probability weighting (RMPW) estimates natural direct and indirect effects by reweighting mediator distributions across treatment conditions rather than modeling the outcome, thereby accommodating treatment-by-mediator interaction. This article brings existing RMPW methods together within a common estimation framework, incorporates a heteroskedastic normal model for continuous mediators, and extends two-step variance estimation to multiple parametric weight components. The framework is illustrated using a national health survey to decompose disparities in cigarette smoking by sexual-minority status and a randomized welfare-to-work experiment to examine pathways from program assignment through employment to maternal depressive symptoms. Targeted simulations evaluate model specification, alternative weighting strategies, treatment-selection adjustment, weight stability, variance estimation, and continuous treatments. Parametric RMPW performed well when models were adequately specified and weights were stable, but correct specification alone did not prevent unstable estimation from concentrated weights. Stratification-based weighting provided some robustness to model misspecification. Standard errors that treated estimated weights as fixed were unreliable, whereas two-step and bootstrap inference performed well under appropriate conditions. The results provide practical guidance for selecting weighting strategies, diagnosing instability, and conducting inference. The methods are implemented in the community-contributed Stata command mmwsmed.

title: Taste or Strategy? Nationalistic Bias and Competitor Penalties in Figure Skating Judging
abstract: Many decisions rest on expert panels whose members have ties to some candidates, and favoritism is hard to tell from shared taste or better information. Using a rich dataset from figure skating, we find evidence of a strategic compatriot premium and a targeted penalty on the compatriot's close rivals. The premium falls along a randomly drawn start order and, before 2022/23, rises when close rivals have their own judges on the panel. The penalty grows with the compatriot's placement chances and fades once she is out of contention. A counterfactual analysis shows that these biases can shape close competitions.

title: Strategic Causal Policy Learning with Manipulable Eligibility
abstract: The standard rule in unconstrained causal policy learning is simple: treat individuals with nonnegative CATEs. But this rule can fail when treatment eligibility is strategically manipulable. After a policy is announced, individuals may change the covariates used for assignment without changing their underlying treatment effects. We study how such responses affect treatment allocation and welfare. Using an access-burden representation, we characterize strategic treatment and decompose welfare loss into missed beneficial treatment and harmful treatment. For linear CATEs and quadratic manipulation costs, we derive closed-form threshold corrections. When manipulation costs are homogeneous, a single correction recovers the ideal positive-CATE allocation. With heterogeneous costs, welfare maximization, pointwise safety, and minimax group welfare regret can favor different thresholds. Simulations illustrate these tradeoffs and examine the effects of estimating treatment effects and behavioral responses.

title: On the Nonemptiness of the Core: Connecting Cooperative Games and Asset Pricing
abstract: We show that the Bondareva--Shapley theorem for infinite cooperative games can be derived from a version of the fundamental theorem of asset pricing. The link is the Choquet extension of a game, viewed as a possibly nonlinear pricing rule on the space of measurable simple payoffs. Under this identification, balancedness translates into no arbitrage, and a linear functional dominated by the pricing rule yields an allocation in the anti-core; the core statement follows by duality. Applying the arbitrage-free pricing theorem of Cornet (2025), we recover the characterization of the nonvacuity of the core initiated by Schmeidler (1967) and established in full generality by Bartl and Pinter (2023) for bounded-below games. Unlike the earlier derivation in Cornet (2025), our argument does not require the game to have bounded variation or the collection of coalitions to be a $\sigma$-algebra.

title: Causal Learning with Invalid Instruments for High-dimensional Imaging Responses
abstract: Large-scale neuroimaging studies provide high-dimensional imaging phenotypes for understanding brain-related diseases and their causal relations with biological risk factors. While instrumental variable (IV) methods can address unmeasured confounding in such observational data, existing IV methods face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional imaging data, particularly in handling large-scale data and leveraging the intrinsic spatial structure of images. To address these challenges, we propose High-dimensional Functional-imaging Instrumental Variable Estimation (Hi-FIVE), a novel framework for estimating spatially varying causal effects when a majority of the candidate instruments may be locally invalid. We first establish identifiability conditions under which the spatial continuity of the causal effect surface propagates identification from regions where valid instruments form a plurality into regions where they do not, provided that invalid-IV effects switch on non-smoothly. Motivated by this result, Hi-FIVE combines penalized multivariate splines over triangulations for the causal surface and region-wise penalties for spatially localized invalid-IV effects, under an anchor constraint that keeps at least one relevant instrument valid on every simplex. A distributed algorithm parallelizes the computation over simplices for two- and three-dimensional images. We study the asymptotic properties of Hi-FIVE, establish consistency and pointwise asymptotic normality, and construct bootstrap-calibrated simultaneous confidence regions whose finite-sample coverage is evaluated through simulations. Hi-FIVE is illustrated with an analysis of the effect of phosphorylated tau on FDG-PET imaging in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, interpreted under the stated IV assumptions.

title: Prediction-Powered LLM Ranking with Adaptively Collected Human Feedback
abstract: Ranking large language models (LLMs) through human evaluations is essential for downstream decision-making. Because human feedback is expensive, evaluation platforms often collect it adaptively, prioritizing informative model comparisons using previously observed feedback. To further improve precision with limited human feedback, evaluators can draw on abundant unrated responses and relatively inexpensive LLM judges; however, judge bias and adaptive dependence challenge standard i.i.d. inference frameworks. We propose Prediction-Powered Ranking (PP-Rank), a framework that combines LLM-judge predictions with human feedback to improve precision while providing valid inference under adaptive sampling. Data-driven prediction weights minimize the asymptotic covariance trace within the proposed class. In theory, we establish asymptotic normality for general evaluation targets and simultaneous ranking inference. A joint martingale analysis handles dependence between adaptive human feedback and auxiliary data. We further derive a rule for reducing exploration that prioritizes lower-cost comparisons while matching a conservative variance bound, and characterize allocation limits for regular $\sqrt{T}$-rate estimation of pairwise means. Semi-synthetic experiments on UltraFeedback-Extended show improvements over human-only baselines in score estimation, confidence interval width, and ranking certification. Synthetic experiments demonstrate robustness to judge quality and adaptive allocation, while showing that PP-Rank can substantially reduce evaluation costs without sacrificing precision.

title: Identification, estimation, and robust inference of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data
abstract: Many modern datasets such as cross-country panels have a multidimensional structure. Conventional approaches on structural vector autoregressions for identifying structural shocks are not directly suited to these settings where data are naturally organized as matrices or tensors, since the number of parameters grows rapidly and identifying restrictions become hard to impose. We introduce a class of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data that achieves tractability and global identification by assuming a Kronecker structure on the model coefficients. We develop a minimum-distance estimator and establish its asymptotic distribution. To accommodate approximate Kronecker separability, we develop confidence intervals for the structural impulse response functions that are robust to local misspecification, and we show their asymptotic validity. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the validity of the asymptotic approximations and good finite-sample performance of the estimator and their (robust) confidence intervals. We illustrate the methods on a country panel dataset to analyze the dynamic and spillover effects of US monetary policy shocks.

title: Useful Work Can Increase Energy Use: Demand Elasticity and Proof of Useful Work
abstract: A serious criticism of Bitcoin's Proof-of-Work is its enormous electricity consumption. Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW), introduced by Ball, Rosen, Sabin, and Vasudevan (2017), in which mining performs useful computations, was suggested as an alternative to reduce electricity expenditure, with matrix multiplication (MatMul) as a recent concrete instantiation by Komargodski and Weinstein (2026). Perhaps surprisingly, we show that switching to PoUW may increase the total electricity consumption, echoing Jevons' paradox. Intuitively, the PoUW mechanism acts as a subsidy that lowers the effective price of the useful work. Recall that demand is elastic if a discount of x percent in the price leads to an increase of more than x percent in the quantity demanded. If demand is elastic, the resulting increase in quantity demanded leads to a net increase in total electricity consumption; if inelastic, total electricity consumption decreases. Even then, the electricity consumption due to PoUW never vanishes, since the mining subsidy is spent on useful work that would not have been produced without the subsidy. This result is proved in a simple model with electricity-only costs, no PoUW overhead, and an unchanged mining subsidy. The analysis extends to less restrictive settings with adjusted thresholds.

title: Change-point analysis of textual data: a flexible approach
abstract: We propose a CUSUM-based change-point procedure for word-frequency vectors that accounts for the variation in the amount of observed textual information over time. Under a multinomial model, we derive the asymptotic null distribution of the proposed statistic, allowing for varying document numbers and lengths. With trimming based on cumulative word counts, the limiting null distribution does not depend on the temporal distribution of textual information. We also consider parametric and nonparametric bootstrap procedures for finite-sample calibration. A simulation study examines their performance under both multinomial sampling and Dirichlet mixtures of multinomial distributions. The results demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach under increasing document intensity and show that resampling entire documents provides more reliable calibration in the presence of document-level heterogeneity. Finally, we apply the procedure, combined with binary segmentation, to 68,542 abstracts from the arXiv category stat.ML spanning 2007-2025, identifying multiple changes in word-usage patterns.

title: Elicitation of the parameters of a multi-criteria sorting model
abstract: Multiple-criteria decision aiding (MCDA) proposes models and methods for different types of decision problems such as choice, ranking or sorting. Such models involve various parameters that must be elicited. In the elicitation process, all necessary information has to be taken from the decision-maker. For this, several direct and indirect elicitation methods are suggested in the literature. In this work, we concentrate on direct elicitation: we aim at providing a rigorous elicitation procedure for the parameters of the Non-Compensatory Sorting model (NCS), which has been characterized by an axiomatic analysis. A basic version of the NCS model is considered, i.e., a model with two categories and no vetoes. The parameters are the set of sufficient coalitions of criteria and the profile separating the two categories. Regarding the sufficient coalitions, we propose several questioning algorithms that engraft questions on classical graph exploration algorithms such as depth-first search. Such algorithms are implemented and evaluated by simulation. For eliciting the limit profile, we design a questioning algorithm using dichotomy. Questioning algorithms can be optimal in the worst case or on average. An optimal algorithm in the worst case has been proposed by Hansel in the framework of monotone Boolean functions. We implement and evaluate this algorithm as a variant of the depth-first search approaches. Regarding optimal questioning strategies on average, we evaluate decision trees for up to four criteria. On the other hand, we assess how more general is NCS as compared to MR-Sort, a particular case of the NCS model in which sufficient coalitions can be represented by additive weights.

title: Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time
abstract: We study the fair allocation of indivisible items to agents with budget constraints and additive valuations. Each agent compares its own bundle with the subsets of another bundle that fit its budget. An allocation is envy-free up to one item (EF1) if, for every agent and every nonempty subset under comparison, removing an item of maximum value to that agent eliminates its envy. We require EF1 both between agents and towards the charity, which contains all unallocated items. EF1 allocations exist, but computing them in polynomial time has remained open even for homogeneous valuations. We resolve this problem with a polynomial-time algorithm for EF1 allocations under heterogeneous valuations. We also prove that detecting an EF1 violation is NP-complete. Equivalently, checking whether a given allocation is EF1 is coNP-complete. Finally, we give polynomial-time algorithms for envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) both when each agent's valuation is proportional to item size and when each agent has a fixed number of distinct positive item values. As an application, for homogeneous valuations and any $\varepsilon>0$, we obtain an EF1 allocation with at least a $(1/2-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the maximum social welfare in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$.

title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks
abstract: Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment--spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment--exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz--Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.

title: Spatially varying quantile downscaling of summer temperature from atmospheric circulation and long-term trends over peninsular Spain
abstract: Over recent decades, high temperatures have intensified worldwide, with impacts on human health, ecosystems, and the economy. Understanding their spatial evolution requires accounting for long-term temperature changes and the role of atmospheric circulation. Quantile regression provides a flexible framework for characterizing changes across the temperature distribution, with relevance to extremes. We analyze the spatio-temporal evolution of the 0.50 and 0.95 quantiles of daily maximum temperature during summer (June--August) over peninsular Spain from 1960 to 2023. We develop a Bayesian spatially varying quantile regression model for observations from 40 meteorological stations, using ERA5 geopotential fields at tropospheric levels to characterize atmospheric circulation, together with long-term temporal trends capturing the background climate change signal. The spatially varying coefficients allow the sensitivity of temperature to atmospheric circulation to differ across the region, linking synoptic dynamics with local temperature variability. The model separates changes associated with the dynamical atmospheric state from the long-term thermodynamic warming signal, while allowing their effects to vary across the temperature distribution. Results show that atmospheric circulation and long-term trends provide comparable contributions to the observed warming. Significant increases in median and upper-quantile temperatures are found across much of peninsular Spain, with pronounced heterogeneity across months and space, followed by quantiles

title: Near-Purity Screening and Dominant-Atom Estimation in Softmax Mixtures and Their Ensembles
abstract: We study near-purity screening and dominant-atom estimation in softmax mixtures, whose components share a common set of category features. A mixture is called $\varepsilon$-pure if one of its mixing weights is at least $1-\varepsilon$. We introduce the Trace of Latent Covariance Criterion ($\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$), a direct estimator of the trace of the covariance matrix of the latent mixing measure, constructed without estimating its atoms or weights, or knowing the number of components. Unlike existing moment-based approaches, our estimator is constructed for the softmax family and does not require knowledge or estimation of the feature distribution. We establish finite-sample guarantees for $\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$, showing that it achieves a parametric convergence rate up to an additive approximation error of order $p^{-1/2}$, without requiring minimum separation between mixture atoms. We also study estimation of the dominant atom in near-pure mixtures by fitting a single softmax component. We prove that the resulting maximum likelihood estimator has an error bound consisting of the usual parametric term and a bias term governed by the weighted distances between the dominant and remaining atoms, revealing adaptation to the geometry of the mixture. Finally, we extend near-purity screening and dominant-atom estimation to ensembles of softmax mixtures with shared atoms and mixture-specific weights. We apply $\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$ separately to each ensemble member to screen for near-purity without knowing the number of components. Under additional assumptions, clustering the resulting dominant-atom estimators yields finite-sample guarantees for estimating the shared atoms. An application to the Million Song Dataset illustrates how the estimated softmax directions reveal interpretable structure in the data.

title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
authors: (2) The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center)
abstract: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.

title: Modeling inter-exceedance times of extreme heat days
abstract: Extreme heat days, here defined as exceedances of a local calendar-day-based 95% quantile, often occur in clusters forming multi-day heatwaves. A calendar-day based threshold allows for the detection of temperature extremes across all seasons, which may impact several economic sectors, public health and ecosystems. Previous approaches to modeling the occurrences of extreme heat events typically treat heat event duration and the time between heat events separately. We propose modeling the inter-exceedance times (IETs) between extreme heat days, allowing for a unified description within a single model. We consider several candidate distributions for the IETs of extreme heat days and find that the zero-inflated discrete Weibull (ZIDW) distribution clearly provides the best fit according to Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests. The ZIDW distribution is a flexible model for count data exhibiting excess zeros as well as over- and under-dispersion: the zero-inflation component captures the pronounced clustering of heat days, while the discrete Weibull component adequately accounts for over-dispersion. Heat days are extracted using both trend-adjusted and non-trend-adjusted thresholds. This allows the analysis of general changes in the occurrence of extreme heat days as well as changes after accounting for the general increase in temperature.

title: Bias in Method-of-Moments Heritability Estimation Under Model Misspecification
abstract: Method-of-Moments (MoM) based approaches for estimation of variance components --- heritability and beyond --- are central in computational genetics due to their flexibility in addressing diverse and complex models while minimizing assumptions, and ease of computation and approximation in biobank-scale data. MoM are closely related to other important methods in this area like LD-score regression. A fundamental, highly debated question relates to the bias inherent in MoM estimates of variance components when the fitted model is misspecified: since the true underlying model is unknown, the fitted model may be missing some of the components from the true model or contain superfluous ones. We offer a general mathematical formulation of this bias and investigate its properties. This leads to novel insights about the sign and the magnitude of the bias in settings of interest and allows extensions and re-interpretation of previous MoM results in the literature. One case study we pursue is in estimating gene-environment interaction variance components (GxE). We prove that when omitting environment-specific noise components (NxE), the resulting GxE estimates are strictly upward biased, even when no true interaction exists. In another case study, we consider heritability estimation, when the genetic variance components are incorrectly partitioned (such as using a single genome-wide component instead of chromosome-specific components). We derive explicit expressions for the bias in the estimate of genome-wide heritability and its dependence on LD scores within and between components. For example, if all components have the same average LD score, the misspecified heritability estimate is still unbiased.

title: Graph-Guided Bayesian Factor Analysis: A Fast Integrated EFA-CFA Approach for High-Dimensional Data
abstract: Factor analysis has been central to the analysis of high-dimensional biomedical data. However, existing exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis methods face several limitations: less interpretable factor findings, difficulty in identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors, challenges in estimating the covariance among factors, and maximum-likelihood fits that break down when variables outnumber subjects. We propose graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis (gg-BFA) to address these gaps. We first use a Bayesian model to explore and learn the latent graph structure, identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors and how many factors are needed. A dense-subgraph search proposes partitions of the variables into communities, each defining one factor, and a forward stepwise search compares their fractional variational posteriors and stops when the evidence lower bound first decreases. We show that this search recovers the true communities even when the number of variables grows much faster than the sample size. We then develop a confirmatory Bayesian model whose variational posterior of the covariance contracts at the parametric rate up to a logarithmic factor, yielding posterior inference for the factors and their covariance, as well as predictions of missing values. Its four members range from a community mask to several cross-loadings per variable. In five biomedical panels, the complete analysis took under ten minutes each on one GPU, and cross-loadings improved held-out covariance and the prediction of masked measurements. In TCGA Kidney, six of the first eight factors were enriched for known pathways, and 190 of the 210 factor correlations had 95% credible intervals excluding zero. Overall, gg-BFA is computationally fast and provides interpretable factor analysis findings and reliable inference results.

title: Learning Global Equilibria in Non-Concave Prospect Theoretic Games
abstract: Human agents in non cooperative games often exhibit non rational behaviour. Prospect theory provides a behavioural framework to capture how agents perceive gains and losses under risk, but, its incorporation into games typically leads to non concave and non convex utility functions, making equilibrium computation challenging. In such cases, it is difficult to obtain algorithms that have global convergence behaviour. This paper proposes a learning algorithm which uses minorization-maximization (MM). Under a proximal Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition on the potential function, we establish global convergence of the algorithm to a potential-maximizing Nash equilibrium. We further show how the structure of the MM minorizer can be used to enable a distributed implementation of the algorithm. With additional noise injection, the individual updates of the agents can be obscured, while still ensuring global convergence.

title: That Time of the Year Again: Government Pay Revisions in the Aggregate Economy
abstract: Public pay is set by law in nominal terms, so inflation erodes its real value between legal acts until the government revises it. I model each revision as the choice of a forward-looking government, shaped by two costs that push in opposite directions. A fixed cost of acting makes revisions large and rare, whereas a convex cost of financing the increase at once makes them small and frequent. Through the budget, each revision also moves debt and the risk of fiscal stress under which the next one is made. In the documented pay decisions of eleven countries, pay set at discretion erodes against prices and private earnings and is restored in discrete steps, every cut was decided during market stress or an adjustment program, and court rulings drove a wedge between the cuts legislated, the cuts paid and the cuts that lasted. Estimated on the legal acts, the model reproduces the documented paths of pay in most countries when data and simulations are measured the same way. In Portugal's estimated model, the savings that the Treasury requires once spreads rise produce the cuts, the debt overhang holds pay down after the crisis, and a court that strikes cuts after they take effect invites cuts it will strike. Review of cuts before they took effect would have lowered the social cost of Portugal's crisis relative to review after the fact, and partial indexation would have paid in Bangladesh unless its automatic increases were costly to finance.

title: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Resource Allocation under Institutional Asymmetry
abstract: We develop a two-player knapsack game to investigate resource allocation under individual capacity constraints, competition over shared resources, and institutional asymmetry. Players select feasible subsets of resources, while their payoffs depend on competitive losses, allocation rules, and asymmetric institutional benefits and costs. We derive the aggregate welfare function and show that allocation coefficients redistribute payoffs without directly affecting total welfare, whereas institutional parameters influence welfare through their net contribution. Consequently, institutional arrangements with identical welfare effects may induce different strategic incentives and Nash equilibrium outcomes. We analyze how capacity constraints and institutional priority shape equilibrium configurations and their welfare properties. A central result concerns the distinction between the social efficiency and strategic stability of shared resources. We derive conditions under which sharing is socially preferable to exclusive allocation yet remains strategically unstable because the non-priority player can increase their payoff by abandoning the resource. Conversely, sharing may remain strategically stable even when exclusive allocation yields higher aggregate welfare. These findings demonstrate that social efficiency and strategic stability need not coincide under institutional asymmetry.

title: Robust Posterior Projection for Bayesian Inference Under Order Restrictions
abstract: In archaeology and geochronology, stratigraphic information constrains the relative chronological order of dated samples. Bayesian chronological models incorporate these constraints either through the prior, or by projecting an unconstrained posterior distribution onto the set of ordered chronologies. Dating measurements may nevertheless appear inconsistent with their stratigraphic position, owing to disturbances that do not justify discarding them. We introduce different robust projection maps based on the Huber loss and characterize the non-uniqueness of the considered maps which justifies a Tikhonov regularization. The robust maps also decompose each sample into a monotone baseline and a spike, which flags questionable samples. We adapt the Sequential Block Merging algorithm for the Huber-type losses, and propose a data-driven heuristic for selecting the hyperparameter on which each loss depends on. Simulation studies and geochronological case studies illustrate the gains in robustness and their limits.

title: Fiscal Commitment and the Additionality of Philanthropy: Heterogeneous Donor Purposes in a Shared Public Budget
abstract: Philanthropic donors often value different public services, while a budget authority allocates public spending across a shared portfolio. Policy frameworks frequently seek to ensure that private finance supplements rather than displaces public funding. We distinguish baseline additionality, which preserves pre-gift public funding, from portfolio preservation, which preserves a service's provision after all gifts are pooled under discretionary budgeting. A larger gift to one service raises the discretionary provision of every service and reduces the protection slack available to the others. This cross-donor fiscal externality yields an exact feasibility result: if a service's maximum permissible floor lies below its discretionary post-gift provision, every effective protection reform reduces that service relative to the portfolio reference, including full protection of its own appropriation. Conversely, a reform that expands at least one donor-backed service while preserving all others exists exactly when every maximum floor reaches the reference. The paper characterizes the complete preservation set and its welfare-maximizing element. Under logarithmic preferences, donation shares determine protectability, while heterogeneous donor valuations determine welfare incidence. Baseline additionality may therefore hold while a service loses fiscal benefits generated by other gifts.

title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series
abstract: Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.

title: Numerical and analytical strategies to propagate correlated uncertainties through the discrete Fourier transform
authors: Tuguldur Zolzaya and Andrew R. McCluskey
abstract: The Fourier transform underpins a range of comparisons between atomistic simulations and scattering measurements, yet uncertainty propagation through it is seldom discussed, and correlations between data points are usually ignored. Here, we give a pedagogical account of uncertainty propagation through the discrete Fourier transform, including the full covariance matrix. Two routes are described: a numerical scheme that samples from the multivariate normal distribution describing the data, and an analytical scheme that treats the transform as a change of basis. We discuss the scaling behaviour of these methods and demonstrate their utility on problems that link simulation to scattering: the Faber--Ziman partial structure factors of liquid water, and the dynamic structure factor obtained from a rotational autocorrelation function.

title: TRACE: Adaptive Credibility Reweighting for Robust Bayesian Model Selection with Source Summary Statistics
abstract: This study focuses on regression estimation and variable selection based on target data, while incorporating information from coefficient estimates obtained in related studies. A weighted combination of these estimates may agree with some target effects but differ from others. We propose Transfer Regression with Adaptive Credibility Estimation (TRACE), a Bayesian method requiring only fitted coefficients and sample sizes from source studies. TRACE learns simplex-constrained source weights shared across variables. Separate latent indicators determine target inclusion and whether each coefficient is guided by the weighted source estimate. We develop an approximate collapsed variational expectation-maximization algorithm with robust source-weight initialization. Under suitable conditions, consistency of variable selection, transfer decisions, and source-weight estimation is established. These results hold at every prespecified fixed iteration in fixed dimension and at global mean-field optima of the exact collapsed variational objective as the dimension grows. Simulations show that TRACE achieves competitive variable-selection performance under different patterns of source heterogeneity. An application to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression project illustrates its use in cross-tissue gene-expression prediction.

title: Fueling Inflation Risks: An Oil Shortage Scenario
abstract: Central banks routinely use alternative scenarios to assess risks to the economic outlook, but these are usually generated from linear models that are unable to speak to the likelihood of extreme outcomes. We develop a nonlinear modeling framework that turns a narrative oil market scenario into a fully probabilistic assessment of the dynamics of oil and gasoline prices, aggregate inflation, and household inflation expectations. It combines an expert-based path for a tail event, a nonparametric model of the global oil market, and nonlinear Phillips curves for the energy, food, and core components of PCE inflation. We apply it in real time to quantify energy price and inflation risks of a severe oil shortage caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, modeled as a rapid drawdown of global petroleum inventories, using only information available in February 2026. Our analysis shows that once oil reserves hit rock bottom, oil and gasoline prices rise sharply, with risks tilted to the upside. Headline PCE inflation peaks near 4.8% in late 2026, and households expect inflation to rise by about 3 percentage points. Two years out, inflation is still highly likely to exceed the Fed's 2% target.

title: The Fragility Of Synthetic Populations Over Time: An Evaluation Of Forecasting Strategies For Agent-Based Models
abstract: Agent-based simulation models are widely used to assess the future mobility projects. However, their effectiveness hinges on the accuracy of synthetic populations, which are often generated using data from a single reference year. This study explores the temporal validity of these populations by evaluating their performance over multi-year datasets in a simulation-like environment. We focus on multi-dimensional agents, ensuring that all attributes critical to the simulation are comprehensively represented. To assess the quality of synthetic populations, we compare three generation methods: direct use of original training data, Bayesian Network sampling, and diffusion model. We then evaluate four agent-forecasting approaches: static projection (both idealistic and realistic), resampling, and dynamic projection. While dynamic projection holds potential, it requires complex longitudinal data to model the evolution of agent attributes. To address this, we introduce a heuristic model based on aggregated statistics, though its limitation lies in ignoring attribute correlations, which reduces its accuracy. Our results demonstrate that synthetic populations lose relevance over time, emphasizing the necessity of effective agent-forecasting. Among the methods tested, idealistic static projection yields the best performance but requires data that is difficult to obtain. The other methods show limited improvements, highlighting the ongoing challenges in accurately forecasting agent attributes.

title: The role of administrative costs in policies to improve cooperation
abstract: We use an agent-based model for studying policies of an abstract government to increase the level of cooperation. In situations where defection is the rational choice, agents receive a bonus if they choose to cooperate. The government taxes agents' payoffs from a repeated prisoner's dilemma game to establish a budget that covers the payment of bonuses, but also the administrative costs involved. We consider costs to identify cooperators, and costs to mitigate the consequences of defective behavior. Governmental interventions are fallible, i.e. cooperators and defectors are correctly identified only with a certain accuracy. Hence, the critical bonus needed to let agents cooperate depends on the accuracy, but also on the current level of cooperation. We analyze the cost constraints for the government to pay the critical bonus and different policies to adjust the accuracy dependent on the level of cooperation. We find that perfect cooperation becomes impossible. Instead, high levels of cooperation can be achieved with optimal adjustment policies.

title: Inequality-Aware Regulation
abstract: I study regulation of a screening monopolist when the regulator cares about the distribution of surplus across heterogeneous consumers and the firm. Consumers privately know their willingness to pay for quality, and the firm privately knows its production costs. Regulatory contracts specify quality-price options that the firm must offer. I show that when the regulator gives greater weight to consumers with lower willingness to pay, baseline regulation is optimal: the regulator requires affordable basic options but leaves the firm free to design and price premium options. Under strong consumer-side redistributive concerns, a single required basic option suffices. The regulator uses the firm's incentive to extract surplus from premium buyers to support low regulated prices for basic options.

title: Algorithm-aware Statistical Inference in High-dimensional Estimating Equations
abstract: Iterative algorithms are integral to many statistical procedures, whereas sampling uncertainty along their iteration is generally not quantified. We develop simultaneous inference for discrete trajectories generated from high-dimensional estimating equations, with iteration-specific population estimands that preserve algorithmic regularization. Our proposed fixed-Jacobian bootstrap propagates perturbations along the observed trajectory without repeatedly running the original nonlinear algorithm. We establish uniform first-order expansions and bootstrap validity over possibly infinite sets of contrasts and iterations under stability, entropy and moment conditions. Simulations in sparse linear regression, paired Fisher discrimination, and temporal-difference learning demonstrate accurate simultaneous coverage. A micro-randomized trial application illustrates inference for a treatment trajectory with participant-level clustering.

title: Data-Adaptive Subset-Size Selection for Minimum Covariance Determinant Estimation
abstract: Subset size determines the balance between robustness and efficiency in minimum covariance determinant estimation. Conventional choices fix this balance before the extent and structure of contamination are known. Reweighting does not remove the influence of the initial subset size. We propose a data-adaptive rule based on ordered squared Mahalanobis distances. It selects the first window maximum, with window width proportional to the sample size. For a minimum covariance determinant subset, the statistic equals the smallest squared distance among excluded observations. For smooth elliptical distributions with small one-point contamination, we characterize the first population window maximum. Under suitable conditions, it is the last retained fraction at which excluding the contaminating point remains optimal. We derive a first-order expansion for this boundary and establish sample localization along the full integer path. Without contamination, the selected fraction tends to one. A fast depth-based implementation reuses one ordering across candidate sizes. Simulations under Gaussian and heavy-tailed sampling show gains over fixed subset sizes, most consistently for scatter estimation. Real data analyses show that the initial subset size affects which observations are retained after reweighting.

title: When the Norm is Wrong: Social Norm Misspecification and Targeting with an Application to Microfinance Adoption
abstract: Structural models of peer effects typically capture peer influence through the average, aggregate, or in some cases through extreme peer actions. Such specifications, however, are imposed ex ante and are typically ad hoc. We study the consequences of social norm misspecification by extending the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) norm from continuous to discrete choices. Considering a binary-choice game with incomplete information, we derive results on existence and uniqueness of a rational expectations equilibrium and establish conditions for identification of the structural parameters. We estimate the model by the Nested Pseudo-Likelihood estimator, implemented using the spectral algorithm. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CES estimates of the peer effects approach their true values as the sample grows, whereas imposing a linear norm biases them even in large samples. We apply the framework to microfinance adoption in India and find a strongly max-leaning norm, with significant heterogeneity in curvature and peer effects across villages grouped by caste composition and wealth. In a counterfactual exercise that allocates a fixed subsidy budget to maximise adoption, the estimated and linear norms target very different households, with the former favouring village "leaders", who are more likely to adopt and were the first to be informed about microfinance.

title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting
abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole's radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map's posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.

title: Zero-inflated generalized linear latent variable models for microbiome compositional data
abstract: In this paper, we incorporate the Dirichlet--multinomial distribution into the generalized linear latent variable model (GLLVM) framework to accommodate high-dimensional, overdispersed compositional count data and capture complex covariation among taxa with a low-rank structure. Advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have generated large amounts of microbiome count data, stimulating research into their associations with human diseases and traits. Such data are compositional and often highly sparse for various reasons, posing challenges for statistical analysis. Conventional zero-replacement approaches ignore the underlying causes of zeros, further complicating the analysis. We therefore propose a zero-inflated Dirichlet--multinomial latent variable model (ZIDM-LVM). Since the marginal likelihood has no closed-form expression, we develop a variational approximation (VA) approach for efficient parameter estimation. Simulation studies and applications to two microbiome datasets are presented to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.

title: Individual incentives and uniform gains under symmetric constraints
abstract: We study the division of a fixed total under symmetric joint constraints when agents have continuous, strictly single-peaked preferences over their own shares. Each agent reports a complete preference, including comparisons across the two sides of her peak. For any finite population and any nonempty closed convex permutation-invariant feasible set, we characterize the uniform-gains rule by efficiency, symmetry, individual strategy-proofness, and own-coordinate peak-onlyness. The last condition requires that a change of preference leaving an agent's peak fixed also leave her own share fixed; it places no direct restriction on others' shares. The characterization separates uniqueness from continuity and yields a continuous characterization with individual incentives for compact feasible sets that are polyhedral or relatively full-dimensional and strictly convex. We then show that, for every population of two through six agents and every nonempty compact convex permutation-invariant feasible set, efficiency, symmetry, and individual strategy-proofness alone characterize uniform gains. The proof recovers allocations from the shares attainable by unilateral reports, feasible transfers, and endpoint reports. A common induction applies at each population, with additional starting configurations for five and six agents.

title: Does fare communication format matter? Evidence from a randomised experiment in public transport
abstract: Highly concentrated demand in public transport places pressure on infrastructure and reduces service quality. Pricing instruments-such as discounted off-peak single fare tickets-are a widely used tool for rescheduling demand across time. Yet no study has directly examined whether the price communication format of single fare tickets affects travel behaviour in terms of departure-time rescheduling. To fill this gap, we exploit a randomised stated preference survey conducted in Switzerland based on participants' actual journeys (n = 1,082), assigning participants to one of three price formats: absolute amounts, absolute deviations, or percentage deviations from their current fare. Estimating a multinomial logit model with price-format interaction terms, we find no significant effect of communication format on aggregate price sensitivity. However, for low-fare trips, percentage-based communication substantially amplifies price sensitivity relative to absolute amounts or absolute deviations. Moreover, when prices are shown as percentage deviations, price sensitivity increases for small price spreads and decreases for large price spreads, with a crossover point corresponding to a discount depth of approximately 47%. In summary, these findings suggest that percentage-based price communication has the potential to reinforce the demand-shifting effect of off-peak discounts, particularly for low-fare products and for discounts shallower than approximately 47%.

title: Short-term associations between wild-bird and mammalian high pathogenic avian influenza detection in the United States
abstract: High pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) detections in mammals have raised concern about repeated wildlife spillover and the targeting of mammalian surveillance. We evaluated whether wild-bird detection records contained short-term explanatory and predictive information about mammalian detections in the United States. Public surveillance records from April 2022 to July 2026 comprised 18,523 wild-bird and 815 mammalian detections. Monthly state-level mammalian counts were analysed using negative-binomial mixed models adjusted for seasonality, preceding mammalian detections and state-level heterogeneity. The selected model contained contemporaneous and one-month-lagged same-state wild-bird counts. A doubling of one plus the contemporaneous wild-bird count was associated with a 57.9% increase in the expected mammalian count (95% CI 43.5-73.8%), and a doubling of the preceding-month count with a 15.9% increase (5.2-27.8%). Bordering-state exposure did not improve fit. In a six-month temporal holdout, adding same-state wild-bird exposure reduced mean absolute error by 23.8% and root mean squared error by 27.9%, although total detections remained overpredicted. After exact-row deduplication, the corresponding effects were 59.7% and 13.3%. Wild-bird surveillance records contained short-term, geographically local information about mammalian HPAI detection activity, but the associations do not establish direct transmission and require further calibration before operational forecasting.

title: Conformal Prediction for Multi-Step Forecasting: Conditional Coverage and Sharp Score Calibration Rates
abstract: Uncertainty quantification in prediction is a central problem in statistics and machine learning. Conformal prediction provides a flexible approach to constructing prediction sets with valid marginal coverage under exchangeability. In this paper, we investigate conformal prediction for both one-step and multi-step forecasting from a single stationary time series, addressing temporal dependence and the additional challenges of joint prediction across multiple horizons. We propose a kernel-based framework, called Time series Residual Analysis for Calibration with Kernels (TRACK), for estimating conditional quantiles of residual scores and constructing prediction sets from rolling-window forecasters. The framework accommodates heterogeneous uncertainty across horizons and accounts for dependence induced by rolling estimation, while allowing predictor memory and forecast horizons to grow with the sample size. Our finite-sample bounds quantify how temporal dependence and overlapping score windows affect calibration and coverage. We further derive bounds for conditional quantile estimation and pointwise conditional coverage discrepancy. The guarantees extend to more general predictors that admit an accurate rolling-window approximation. We also derive matching minimax bounds over classes of known score maps, clarifying how overlapping score windows affect calibration accuracy. Experimental results from simulations and applications to wind energy generation and bike sharing demand show that our methods improve regional conditional coverage while maintaining competitive interval widths.

title: Cluster-weighted modeling for count data with excess zeros and mixed-type covariates
abstract: Count data may exhibit excess zeros, within-group overdispersion, and heterogeneous relationships between the response and its covariates. Conventional zero-inflated regression models typically impose a single count-regression structure, whereas Poisson count components cannot accommodate residual within-component overdispersion. We propose a zero-inflated negative binomial cluster-weighted model that combines a structural-zero component with multiple negative binomial regression components and jointly models the response and mixed-type covariates.We establish sufficient conditions for identifiability of the proposed model and its Poisson counterpart and develop an expectation-maximization algorithm for estimation. Numerical studies demonstrate improved regression coefficient estimation and clustering performance relative to the Poisson counterpart under within-component overdispersion.

title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data
abstract: Functional count data arise when recurrent events are recorded repeatedly over time and scientific interest centers on how event rates evolve over time and across experimental conditions. Standard mixed effects models for counts have interpretable mean structures but require a parametric conditional distribution, which can be restrictive in the presence of overdispersion, unusual zero frequencies and heavy tails. To address these challenges, we develop the functional count DPGLM (fcDPGLM), a semiparametric Bayesian mixed model that combines GLM-style regression with a nonparametric count distribution. Parametric condition-specific mean trajectories and subject-specific random effects determine the conditional mean exactly, allowing the interpretation of contrasts as usual, while remaining details of the count distribution are learned nonparametrically from the data. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models are recovered as limiting cases. A gamma completely random measure representation allows for efficient posterior simulation. In simulations mimicking a rat seizure study, fcDPGLM estimated mean contrasts as accurately as a correctly specified negative-binomial mixed model, and more accurately otherwise, and recovered zero and exceedance probabilities that the parametric models misrepresent. In the seizure study, seizure rates rise and then decline in the early period after induced status epilepticus but remain high and nearly flat in the chronic period, and rats differ substantially. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models estimate similar mean trajectories and period contrasts, but only fcDPGLM matches the observed zero frequency, variance and high-burden days.

title: Characterizing Underrepresentation when Generalizing Causal Survival Estimates
abstract: Randomized trial findings are routinely generalized to broader target populations to inform decisions in medicine and public policy. When the trial sample is misaligned with the target population, generalized effect estimates can yield suboptimal decisions. We characterize the target subgroups that are underrepresented in the trial cohort in time-to-event settings. Here, underrepresentation arises in two distinct ways: baseline underrepresentation, when a subgroup's covariate profile is rare in the trial relative to the target, and time-varying underrepresentation, when differential censoring erodes a subgroup over follow-up. Existing diagnostics either conflate these mechanisms or apply only to the baseline case. We show that the asymptotic variance of the efficient generalizability estimator admits a decomposition in which only two terms can diverge as representation weakens: a sampling-weight term capturing baseline misalignment and a censoring-weight term capturing differential loss to follow-up. Underrepresented subgroups are therefore those with imprecise generalized estimates, and the larger of the two terms gives the responsible channel. We use this decomposition in TRACE (Temporal Rashomon Analysis of CEnsored data), which combines a self-normalized variance objective with a tree-based search to localize underrepresented subgroups, attribute each to baseline mismatch or censoring, and find the follow-up intervals where censoring drives the variance inflation. We solve the joint problem with a parametric dynamic program nested inside a Rashomon ensemble of near-optimal trees. In synthetic benchmarks, TRACE recovers the planted underrepresented regions. In a case study generalizing the National Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) Study to U.S. JTPA-eligible adults, restricting to reliably generalizable subgroups narrows the 95% confidence interval for the refined estimand by 60%.

title: Semiparametric causal mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials with post-treatment confounding
abstract: Causal mediation analysis of cluster-randomized trials can reveal how interventions affect outcomes through individual and spillover pathways. Most existing methods target natural mediation effects under assumptions that exclude treatment-induced mediator--outcome confounding. We develop a semiparametric framework for interventional mediation effects that accommodates such confounding and within-cluster interference without requiring cross-world independence assumptions. We identify cluster-average and individual-average direct and indirect effects and decompose the indirect effect into individual and spillover components, distinguishing pathways through an individual's own mediator and those of other cluster members. These contrasts evaluate hypothetical interventions on the joint mediator distribution and can differ from treatment effects carried through individual causal pathways represented by natural effects, thereby providing an intervention-oriented perspective that complements natural effects. We derive efficient influence functions to construct estimators using cluster-level cross-fitting, characterize their multiple-robustness properties, and establish conditions for asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency. To facilitate implementation, we develop a lower-dimensional reparameterization that reduces the need for multivariate density estimation and integration and allows nuisance functions to be estimated using parametric models or machine learning. Simulation studies evaluate finite-sample performance, and an application to a cluster-randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain illustrates the proposed methods.
